title: How Underwater Tunnels Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how underwater tunnels are built, starting with the reasons to tunnel instead of bridge (ship traffic, air strikes, weight capacity, earthquakes, cost curves). They cover ancient precedents (a Babylonian pedestrian tunnel under the Euphrates), notable modern examples (Seikan Tunnel in Japan, Channel Tunnel between England and France, Marmaray Tunnel in Istanbul and the port of Theodosius found during its digging), and three construction methods: the tunneling shield (Marc Isambard Brunel, inspired by the shipworm, used on the Thames tunnel), the tunnel boring machine, and the immersed tube tunnel (W.J. Wilgus, Detroit River tunnel; Hong Kong-Macau link). The episode ends with listener mail correcting their chess episode on knight jumping, castling restrictions, and pawn promotion.

segments.title: Opening banter and tunnel definitions
segments.summary: Hosts banter and introduce the topic of underwater tunnels, distinguishing a tunnel bored underground from a cut-and-cover conduit, and noting people have built under water since ancient times.

segments.title: Ancient and 19th-century underwater tunneling
segments.summary: The hosts describe a Babylonian pedestrian tunnel under the Euphrates built after the river was diverted, and say serious advances came in the 1800s.

segments.title: Tunnels versus bridges
segments.summary: Hosts compare tunnels and bridges, covering drawbridges and shipping lanes, air strikes, storms and currents, weight capacity, earthquakes, and how cost changes with length.

segments.title: Notable modern underwater tunnels
segments.summary: The Seikan Tunnel between Honshu and Hokkaido in Japan, the Channel Tunnel under the English Channel, and the Marmaray Tunnel in Istanbul, which connects Europe and Asia and uncovered the Port of Theodosius.

segments.title: Tunneling shield and Brunel
segments.summary: Marc Isambard Brunel's tunneling shield, inspired by the shipworm, is explained as a coffee-can-shaped frame where workers dig in compartments while hydraulic jacks advance it and workers line the tunnel behind. The Thames tunnel is mentioned, including its funding shutdown and compressed-air airlocks.

segments.title: Movie tangents
segments.summary: A brief digression on Die Hard with a Vengeance, The Great Escape, and other films, with the hosts discussing tunneling scenes and unrelated movies.

segments.title: Tunnel boring machines
segments.summary: Tunnel boring machines are described as all-in-one machines that cut, support and build as they advance through rock, at roughly 250 feet per day. Two were used on the Channel Tunnel, guided by GPS. Breakdowns are discussed, and a proposed transatlantic tunnel is dismissed as impractical.

segments.title: Immersed tube tunnels
segments.summary: Immersed tube tunnels are built as prefabricated concrete sections floated out, sunk into a dredged trench, joined with rubber gaskets and bulkheads, and covered. W.J. Wilgus pioneered the method with the Detroit River Railroad Tunnel; the Hong Kong-Macau link will include a 6.7 km immersed section.

segments.title: Listener mail on chess
segments.summary: A listener correction on the chess episode: knights can jump pieces, castling is not allowed after either piece has moved or through check, and pawns can only promote to a piece already lost.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners, give social media and email contacts, and sign off.
